papers.title_in_file: Quantum Positional Encodings for Graph Neural Networks
papers.version_note: arXiv:2406.06547v1, the ICML 2024 (PMLR 235) paper, 30 pages with Appendices A to D. The text layer holds the paper twice; the first copy was read and the second used only to check quotes.
papers.what_it_is: A paper by Pasqal authors proposing positional encodings for graph transformers from quantum states built on the graph (ground-state correlations, 1- and 2-particle quantum walks), with expressivity propositions against Weisfeiler-Lehman tests and benchmarks run with classically simulated, tractable versions of the features.

existing.note: The abstract and conclusion say the authors 'prove' greater expressivity on strongly regular graphs, but the proofs in Section 4 and Appendix B establish: a localized single-walker quantum walk is not weaker than 1-WL and is weaker than 2-WL (Prop 4.2); GD-WL with RRWP cannot distinguish SRGs of the same family (Prop 4.6); and the solvable one-layer Ising case cannot either (Prop 4.7). The positive SRG result, that a two-layer Ising evolution and a 2-particle walk distinguish SRGs, is stated as empirical (Section 4.3) and as not yet demonstrated in general. Narrowed to that.
existing.value: The authors state they prove some quantum positional encodings are more expressive than random-walk and Laplacian ones on strongly regular graphs; what the paper proves is that random-walk (RRWP) distances and a one-layer Ising evolution cannot distinguish non-isomorphic strongly regular graphs of the same family, while the distinction of such graphs by a two-layer Ising evolution and a 2-particle quantum walk is shown empirically on two families and stated as not yet demonstrated in general.
existing.anchor: Abstract; Sections 4.2 and 4.3, pp.6 to 7; Section 6, p.9
quotes: We proved that some positional encodings that use quantum features are theoretically more expressive than ones based on simple random walk and laplacian eigenvectors, on strongly regular graphs.
Proposition 4.6. GD-WL with RRWP distance cannot, even with eigen-decomposition of the distance matrix, distinguish non isomorphic SRGs from the same family.
This result shows that the case in which it is possible to derive formal expressions actually fails to distinguish non isomorphic SRGs.
a two layers Ising evolution and a 2-QW are strictly more powerful than 2-WL.
This property has been demonstrated in some cases for k = 1 and observed for k = 2 in the case of SRGs, but not yet demonstrated in the general case and for any value of k.
existing.certainty_reason: The positive SRG result is empirical on two families; the proved results are limits of the classical encodings and of the solvable Ising case.
existing.reader_inference: The 'proof' in the abstract and conclusion is stronger than the body supports: the body proves the classical baseline fails on SRGs and observes that the quantum features succeed on 25 graphs.

quotes: While it remains unclear whether an actual performance improvement will be observed on real-world use cases, and whether this improvement will justify the cost of using quantum hardware in the future
existing.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limit, Section 6, p.9.

quotes: We limited ourselves to versions of quantum features that are efficiently computable and we were able to show a small gain in performance compared to state-of-the-art models.

existing.reader_inference: In Table 1 the gains over the authors' own GRIT run (ZINC 0.058 or 0.059 against 0.060; MNIST 98.204 against 98.164; CIFAR10 76.442 against 76.198) are within one standard deviation, and on PATTERN and CLUSTER the quantum encodings score below that run.

Narrowed to carry this setup.
existing.value: The authors report that on an artificial binary graph classification dataset of 800 ladder-based graphs, built so that their Ising ground states can be computed efficiently, a GCN using eigenvectors of the ground-state correlation matrix reaches 100% test accuracy while classical models with Laplacian eigenvectors or RRWP reach 45% accuracy.

We were able to engineer an artificial dataset for which classical approaches fail to perform the associated binary classification tasks
